input:
When two liquids are mixed together, it is often assumed that they will blend into a single uniform phase, but this is by no means always the case. Certain pairs of liquids dissolve in one another only to a limited extent, and when such a pair is mixed in proportions that fall within the range of limited miscibility, the result is not a single homogeneous liquid but a separation into two distinct liquid phases, each of which is rich in one of the two components and saturated with the other.

The condition that governs the equilibrium between the two phases can be stated in words, without reference to any equation: for each component of the pair, the chemical potential of that component must be the same in both phases. The chemical potential can be thought of as a measure of the tendency of a component to move from one phase to another, and if it is higher in one phase than in the other, the component will tend to transfer into the phase where its potential is lower, and this transfer will continue until the potentials have become equal and the driving force for further transfer has disappeared.

An important consequence of this condition is that the compositions of the two phases are not arbitrary. At a given temperature and pressure, the composition of each phase is fixed by the equilibrium itself, and it does not depend on the proportions in which the two liquids were originally combined. Changing the overall proportions changes the relative amounts of the two phases present, but it leaves the composition of each individual phase unchanged, provided the mixture as a whole remains within the range in which two phases coexist.

Two liquids that dissolve in each other only to a limited extent form a partially miscible pair. Mixed in proportions inside the miscibility gap, such a pair does not give a single homogeneous liquid: it separates into two liquid phases, one rich in the first liquid and the other rich in the second, and the two phases stand in equilibrium with each other.

Equilibrium between the phases has a precise condition, stated here in words before any symbol is attached to it. For each component of the pair, the chemical potential of that component is the same in one phase as in the other, and no net transfer of the component between the phases takes place. If the chemical potential of a component stood higher in one phase than in the other, the component would move into the phase of lower potential until the difference disappeared.

The condition fixes the compositions of the two phases. At a given temperature and pressure, each phase holds a definite composition, set by the equilibrium and not by the proportions in which the liquids were mixed. Adding more of one liquid to the mixture changes the amounts of the two phases, and leaves the composition of each phase unchanged, as long as the overall mixture stays inside the gap. Outside the gap, the pair mixes completely and a single phase results.
